etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift in reading from the kun'yomi of shimobe or yatsugare to use the on'yomi of boku instead, first attested in kundoku contexts from the mid-to-late 1700s and becoming prevalent from around the Meiji period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 下(しも) (shimo, “lower”) + 部(べ) (be, “servant to the imperial court”). First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720, with the spelling 下客.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From older 這(は)ひ入(い)る (fafiiru, modern pronunciation 這(は)い入(い)る (haiiru)), itself a compound of 這(は)ひ (fafi, modern pronunciation 這(は)い (hai), 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 這(は)ふ (fafu, “to crawl”, modern pronunciation 這(は)う (hau))) + 入(い)る (iru, “to enter, to go in”).
* /faɸiiru/ → /fawiiru/ → /faiiru/ → /fairu/ → /hairu/
This shortened hairu form is first attested from the early 1200s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Man'yōshū of 759. Related to 入(い)れる (ireru, “to put in”), its active form.
For the development of the “to be necessary” sense, consider the English phrase to come into it in the sense “to be a factor in something”. In modern usage, this particular sense is more commonly spelled as 要(い)る.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese; see modern form 入(い)れる (ireru) for more.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Regular development of classical 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verb 入(い)る (iru, “to put something into something else”, transitive).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 入る entry.
Active form of 入(い)る (iru, “to enter, to go into something”, intransitive) and its alternative form 要(い)る (iru, “to need, to require”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Regular potential form of verb 入(はい)る (hairu, “to go in, to enter”, intransitive).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 八 (MC peat). Compare literary Hokkien 八 (pat), Hakka 八 (pat).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 八 (ya), from Proto-Japonic *ya.
The ablaut form of 四 (yo, “four”), which it doubles.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 切(き)る (kiru, “cut, slice, carve”) + 符(ふ) (fu, “tally split in half used for identification”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Ainu ペッ (pet, “water, river”). The kanji spelling is an example of ateji.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of 地(ち)下(か)鉄(てつ)道(どう) (chika tetsudō, “underground railway”), itself 地下(ちか) (chika, “underground”) + 鉄道(てつどう) (tetsudō, “railway”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Possibly related to 濡(ぬ)れる (nureru, “to get wet”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 大(だい)学(がく) (daigaku, “university”) + 生(せい) (-sei, “student; pupil”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 客 (MC khaek). Compare modern Hokkien literary reading khik.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: ⟨marepi₁to₂⟩ → */marepʲitə/ → /marefito/ → /marohito/ → /maroːdo/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Also cited to a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 781, with the phonetic spelling 宇志呂 (usiro₂). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *osirə. Cognate with Hachijō おしろ (oshiro).
Ultimate derivation unknown. Might be from stem us- ("lost; gone, out of sight", as in 失う (ushinau, “to lose”), older verb 失す (usu, “to lose; to go away”)) + locative suffix -ro₂ indicating an interior (as in 所 (tokoro, “place”), 空ろ・虚ろ (utsuro, “emptiness, a hollow”), 洞・空・虚 (uro, “a hollow space in something”), 室 (muro, “room; cave”), possibly 心 (kokoro, “heart”)). The earliest sense of "somewhere out of sight" also suggests a connection with stem us-.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived from verb 急ぐ (isogu, “to hurry, to rush, to hasten”).
First attested in a text from 850.
By one analysis, this is the verb's 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete or irrealis form”) 急が (isoga) plus the adjectivizing suffix しい (-shii, “having that kind of quality”, classical terminal form -shi).
Alternatively, may be derived from the causative. The classical terminal form of the adjective is identical to the classical continuative or infinitive form of the causative verb, which was used in certain constructions to conclude sentences.
* 急ぐ (isogu, “to rush, to hurry”) → 急がす (isogasu, “to cause to rush, to cause to hurry”) → 急がし (isogashi, “having the quality of causing one to rush or hurry”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*⟨sepasi⟩ → /seɸaɕi/ → /sewaɕiki/ → /sewaɕiː/
May be cognate with 狭い (sebai), older form of 狭い (semai, “adjective, lacking in space”), expanding on the meaning towards “lacking in time”.
First cited to a text from 1020.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kanasiki₁⟩ → /kanasiki/ → /kanaɕiː/
From Old Japanese 悲し (kanasi-, “emotionally overwhelming: dear, beloved, sad”), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kanasi- (“beloved, dear”). First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Historically also meant "dear; beloved; lovely", in addition to "sad". The former senses were later taken over by other adjectives such as 愛らしい (airashii), 愛しい (itoshii), and 可愛い (kawaii). See also the Ryukyuan cognates such as Miyako かなすぃ゚ (kanasï) and Okinawan かなさん (kanasan, “beloved, lovely, cute”), which do not mean "sad".
Considering the original sense of "emotionally overwhelming", might be cognate with 兼ねる (kaneru, “to group together; to be concerned about something”), from the semantic overlap with grief.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived via regular historical processes from the 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) intransitive form of classical Japanese verb 揺る (yuru), itself from Old Japanese.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 揺る entry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ki no pu/ → /kinoɸu/ → */kinowu/ → /kinou/ → /kinoː/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kinəpu.
The initial ki is unclear, but is likely the same ki element that appears in other words pertaining to the past. This may be related to the now-obsolete auxiliary verb き (ki) indicating the recollective past -- see けり (keri). The middle no appears to be the regular genitive particle の (no). The final pu is an apophonic form of 日 (hi, “day”), also found in 今日 (kepu→kyō, “today”).
Martin suggests that the initial ki might also be related to Old Japanese 來 (ku, “to come”), modern 来る (kuru), presumably via the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of ki. However, this is problematic both semantically, as "the coming day" would presumably refer to tomorrow rather than yesterday; and grammatically, as a verb modifying a noun would be expected to conjugate into the regular attributive form (for 來 (ku) that would be kuru), rather than into the continuative form that then necessitates a particle.
The kanji are orthographic borrowing from Chinese 昨日 (zuórì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 昨日 (dzak nyit, literally “yesterday + day”). Compare modern Cantonese reading zok⁶ jat⁶.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. The initial ki is unclear, but is likely the same ki element that appears in other words pertaining to the past. This may be related to the now-obsolete auxiliary verb き (ki) indicating the recollective past -- see けり (keri). The final so is also unclear, but is probably the same as the final zo in 去年(こぞ) (kozo).
This may have been read as kizo in Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *atu.
Cognate with 熱(あつ)い (atsui, “hot (of an object)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɸiŋɡaɕi/ → /ɸiɡaɕi/ → /hiɡaɕi/
Sound shift from hingashi (see Etymology 2 below).
Now the standard word for east.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*⟨pi₁ muka si⟩ → */pʲimukasi/ → /pimʉɡasi/ → /ɸimʉɡaɕi/ → /ɸiŋɡaɕi/ → /hiŋɡaɕi/
Shift from Old Japanese 東 (*pi₁mukasi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨aduma⟩ → /ad͡zuma/ → /azuma/
From Old Japanese, itself of unknown derivation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 東 (MC tuwng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Mandarin 東 /东 (dōng).
Compare Wu 東 /东 (ton), Hakka 東 /东 (tûng), Min Nan 東 /东 (tong).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of the stem of adjective 明らか (akiraka, “clear”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of verb 上る, 登る (noboru, “to ascend, rise”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 始める (hajimeru, “to begin, start”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 毎 (mai, “every, each”) + 月 (tsuki, “month; moon”).
First attested in the latter 1400s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 毎 (mai, “every, each”) + 月 (getsu, “month; moon”).
First attested in roughly 1215.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Dialectal shift from standard Japanese maitsuki, moving from diphthong /ai/ to monophthong /e/.
* /mait͡suki/ → /met͡suki/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wataru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 漢字 (MC xanH dziH, literally “Han Chinese + character”). Compare modern Mandarin 漢字／汉字 (hànzì), Hokkien 漢字 /汉字 (hàn-jī / hàn-lī).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle Chinese 百 (MC paek, literally “hundred”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/mo₁mo₁/ → /momo/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/po/ → /ɸo/ → /ho/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/po/ → /ɸo/ → /wo/ → /o/
From Old Japanese. Change in pronunciation from ho (see above).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *iku. Cognate with Okinawan 行(い)ちゅん (ichun), Miyako 行きぃ (iksï).
The original Proto‐Japonic root was vowel‐initial, as evidenced by the Ryukyuan cognates. In Old Japanese, a prothetic glide /j/ was often inserted before certain vowel‐initial words to ease pronunciation. This phonological innovation created the variant form 行(ゆ)く (yuku), paralleling the i‐ ~ yu‐ alternation seen in the archaic noun 夢 (ime₂) versus modern 夢(ゆめ) (yume).
Because the innovative yuku form was heavily utilized in foundational classical literature, such as the Man’yōshū, it became fossilized as the high‐prestige, conservative literary standard. Meanwhile, the direct descendant iku persisted as the common spoken vernacular and was ultimately adopted as the standard for modern spoken Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 親切 /亲切 (tshin tshet, literally “blood relative + close”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 門 (MC mwon).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kado₁⟩ → */kadʷo/ → /kado/
From Old Japanese.
The final -do is cognate with 戸(と) (to, “door”). Compare 籠(かご) (kago, “basket”), which is cognate with 籠(こ) (ko).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₁nari⟩ → */tʷonari/ → /tonari/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tonari.
Analyzable as a compound of Old Japanese 外 (to₁, “outside, other”) + nari, possibly the nominalization of verb なる (naru, “to become”), or a contraction of に (ni, locative particle) + あり (ari, copular "to be" verb, predicative and nominal form).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 鄰 (MC lin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 音樂 (MC 'im ngaewH|ngaewk|lak).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in 1908, cited from the 万朝報 (Yorozu Chōho) serial in its October 3 issue.
From 飛行(ひこう) (hikō, “flying, flight”) + 機(き) (-ki, “machine”), a calque of English flying machine.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
